short_summary: Algorithms amplify negative emotions to boost engagement
Social media encourages comparison and insecurity
block_text:
Most people think they’re just scrolling. But behind every swipe, there’s a system watching. Social media algorithms are built to keep you there as long as possible. They don’t care what you see—only that you keep looking. And the fastest way to do that isn’t by making you happy. It’s by making you feel something sharp. 

Algorithms notice what grabs your attention. If you pause on a post that annoys you, or makes you feel left out, the system learns. It shows you more of the same. Not because it wants to upset you, but because it knows: strong emotions glue you to the screen. Anger, envy, insecurity—these are the emotions that make people scroll for hours. The algorithm doesn’t know you. It just knows what keeps you hooked.

This is why, after a long session online, people often feel worse about themselves. You see highlight reels of other people’s lives. You see arguments, outrage, and impossible standards. The algorithm pushes these things because they work. They keep you comparing, doubting, reacting. Over time, this chips away at self-esteem. You start to measure yourself against what you see, even if you know it’s not real. 

It’s not a personal weakness. It’s the design. The more you feel you’re missing out, the more you want to check again. The more you compare, the more you scroll. It’s a loop that’s hard to notice when you’re inside it. But step back, and you see: the system is built to keep you feeling unsettled. That’s how it wins your attention. And that’s why people who step away often say they feel lighter, more themselves, less anxious. They’re not just escaping noise—they’re escaping a machine that profits from their doubt.
